title: U.S. House · Virginia's 5th District
area: Virginia's 5th Congressional District (Southside and Central Virginia, including Lynchburg, Danville, and Charlottesville-area exurbs)

context.text: Incumbent John McGuire defeated Melanie Lucero in the August 4, 2026 Republican primary, 84.4% to 15.6%. Former Rep. Bob Good, whom McGuire defeated in the 2024 Republican primary, did not qualify for the 2026 primary ballot. Tom Perriello, who represented this district in Congress from 2009 to 2011, won the Democratic primary with 79.8% of the vote over Suzanne Krzyzanowski and Robert Tracinski.

summary.text: John McGuire is the Republican incumbent U.S. Representative for Virginia's 5th District, first elected in 2024 after defeating then-Rep. Bob Good in the Republican primary. A former Navy SEAL who founded a fitness-training business, he served in the Virginia House of Delegates from 2018 and briefly in the Virginia Senate before going to Congress. He serves on the Armed Services and Oversight committees and is seeking a second term.

background.text: Born in Richmond, Virginia, in 1968 and graduated from Henrico High School. His official biography says he was raised in Central Virginia, spent part of his early childhood in the foster care system, and was raised by his grandparents.
Served as a U.S. Navy SEAL from 1988 to 1998; his official biography says he was a sniper and sniper instructor.

After leaving the military, founded SEAL Team Physical Training Inc. (SEAL Team PT), a fitness-training business that, according to his official biography, has trained individuals, companies and sports teams.
Elected to the Virginia House of Delegates in 2018 and represented District 56 until 2024.

Won the Republican convention in May 2023 and the November 2023 general election for Virginia Senate District 10, and served in the Senate in 2024. His official biography lists service on the Local Government, Privileges and Elections, and Transportation committees and says he led bills on naloxone in schools and on taxes on veteran retirement pay.

Defeated incumbent Rep. Bob Good in the June 18, 2024 Republican primary, 50.3% to 49.7%, with an endorsement from Donald Trump, and won the November 2024 general election by about 15 percentage points over Democrat Gloria Tinsley Witt.
Took office in January 2025. In the 119th Congress he serves on the House Armed Services Committee and the House Oversight Committee.
According to his official biography, he lives in Goochland, Virginia, with his wife, Tracy; they have raised five children.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (Subcommittees on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation; Health Care and Financial Services; and Military and Foreign Affairs) and the House Committee on Armed Services in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).

candidates.name: Tom Perriello
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 4, 2026 Democratic primary with 79.8% of the vote

summary.text: Tom Perriello is the Democratic nominee for Virginia's 5th District and previously represented it in Congress from 2009 to 2011. A Yale-trained attorney, he went on to international justice and diplomatic work, led the Center for American Progress Action Fund, and served as a State Department special envoy. He won the August 2026 Democratic primary and says his campaign theme is lowering prices and raising wages.

background.text: Born and raised in Albemarle County, Virginia, according to Cardinal News. A 2017 campaign website quoted by Ballotpedia describes him as the youngest of four children of Linda and Vito Perriello.
Earned a B.A. and a J.D. from Yale University, receiving the J.D. in 2001.

Moved to West Africa in 2001 and worked as an advisor to the international prosecutor of the Special Court for Sierra Leone, and on international justice efforts in Kosovo, Darfur and Afghanistan. A 2017 campaign website quoted by Ballotpedia also says he earlier worked on environmental issues and helped lead faith-based anti-poverty organizations.
Won election to Virginia's 5th District as a Democrat in 2008, taking office January 3, 2009, and served on the House Committees on Veterans' Affairs and on Transportation and Infrastructure.
Lost re-election in 2010 to Republican Robert Hurt; Cardinal News reports he attributes the loss to backlash over his vote for the Affordable Care Act in March 2010.

Served as CEO of the Center for American Progress Action Fund and counselor for policy at the Center for American Progress, directed the State Department's 2014 Quadrennial Diplomacy and Development Review, and was appointed by President Obama in 2015 as special envoy for the Great Lakes Region of Africa.
Announced in December 2025 that he would seek his former seat, and won the Democratic primary on August 4, 2026, defeating Suzanne Krzyzanowski and Robert Tracinski.

record.text: As a member of Congress (2009-2011), voted for the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act and the Affordable Care Act, according to his own campaign account of his record.

summary.text: Cooke Harvey is an independent candidate in Virginia's 5th Congressional District who has not previously held office. According to Cville Right Now, he is originally from Delaware, has worked in engineering, surveying and wilderness therapy with at-risk youth, and qualified for the ballot with the required 1,000 signatures. He has said he does not accept monetary donations.

background.text: Originally from Delaware; his experience includes engineering and surveying and work in wilderness therapy with at-risk youth, the vocation that brought him to Virginia. He did not attend a traditional college, according to Cville Right Now.

Gathered the 1,000 certified signatures from registered Virginia voters needed to appear on the November 3, 2026 ballot as an independent. He told Cville Right Now he and the other independent adopted a policy of not accepting monetary donations.

researchNotes: Neither major-party candidate has completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey, and no current (2026) campaign-website statements of priorities were located within the research budget; McGuire's and Perriello's official House and Congress-service records substitute for stated priorities. Independent candidate Cooke Harvey has no Ballotpedia biography and no campaign website was found; his biography rests on one news profile, so the entry is minimal.
